title: Clock frequency vs. chip design philosophy
decision: POWER4 was designed with high clock frequency as a primary goal, achieved through deep pipelining and circuit/custom design rather than relying solely on architectural features.
rationale: The paper argues frequency alone doesn't determine performance, but that combining frequency with a balanced, well-architected system (memory bandwidth, multiple cores) yields greater overall system throughput than chasing frequency in isolation.
outcome: POWER4 achieved multi-GHz frequencies while maintaining a balanced system design intended to avoid bottlenecks elsewhere.
weakest_point: I recall the general theme (frequency is not the only goal, balance matters) but cannot confirm exact framing or that it's called out this way structurally.

title: Single-chip module vs. multi-chip module (MCM) packaging
decision: The paper describes packaging four POWER4 chips (eight cores total) together on a multi-chip module to form a larger SMP building block.
rationale: Packaging multiple chips together allowed fast, low-latency chip-to-chip communication for building larger symmetric multiprocessor systems without going through slower off-module paths.
outcome: The MCM approach enabled systems scaling from a single chip up to 32-way (four MCMs) configurations reportedly discussed in the paper.
weakest_point: Exact numbers (four chips per MCM, resulting core/way counts) may be slightly misremembered; this is somewhat general POWER4 knowledge blended with paper-specific recall.

title: On-chip dual-core design with shared L2
where_in_paper: Chip overview / core and cache hierarchy section
decision: POWER4 placed two processor cores on a single chip sharing an on-chip L2 cache.
rationale: Sharing L2 between two cores was intended to improve efficiency of cache usage and inter-core communication compared to giving each core a private, non-shared L2.
outcome: This became a defining architectural feature of POWER4, described as enabling efficient chip-level multiprocessing.
weakest_point: I am fairly confident of the dual-core-shared-L2 fact from general knowledge, but less sure how the paper frames it as a 'decision with rationale' versus a plain description.

title: RAS (Reliability, Availability, Serviceability) design approach
decision: The paper describes building RAS features (such as error checking/correction, dynamic deallocation of faulty resources) directly into the POWER4 microarchitecture rather than treating reliability as an afterthought.
rationale: Enterprise/server customers require high availability; the designers state RAS must be designed in from the start rather than added later, since retrofitting reliability into a design is less effective.
outcome: POWER4 included various RAS mechanisms integrated into the chip and system design.
weakest_point: I recall this theme exists in POWER4-related IBM literature broadly but am not fully certain of its specific placement or exact wording in this particular paper.
